overview: Shona describes related language communities and historical societies, not one kingdom lasting from 1878 to 1914. This imported outline sits largely north of Zimbabwe and misses the heartland of many examples below. The card follows the named communities; its dates and polygon are not reliable cultural boundaries.

periods.title: Farming and specialist crafts
periods.summary: Shona communities combined cultivation with varied local industries, including Njanja ironworking.

periods.title: Colonial occupation and resistance
periods.summary: British South Africa Company occupation and the wars of 1896 to 1897 transformed political authority.

items.text: In the late nineteenth century, Njanja ironworkers in central Zimbabwe used small furnaces supplied with air by bellows through clay pipes. They worked with ore from the Hwedza Mountains. Their achievement lay in controlling a demanding process and producing useful iron tools, not simply finding a rock that looked metallic.

Ironworking also taught skills. Young men could apprentice to Njanja ironmasters, contributing labor while learning the craft. These specialists still farmed, and their workshops depended on relatives and wider networks. A skilled smith could gain followers and influence as well as produce hoes for the next agricultural season.

Nineteenth-century grain storage in southern Zimbabwe offers a regional comparison involving several neighboring peoples, including Karanga and Kalanga communities. At the Homba Hills, builders combined wooden poles and reeds with clay plaster to make bins in protected caves. Keeping a harvest safe required construction skills as well as successful farming.

Some Homba Hills bins were repaired by covering cracks with another layer of clay. This suggests repeated care and reuse. The study links concealed storage with both food security and conflict, but archaeology cannot tell us whether a particular bin was always full or exactly which household depended on it.

Manyika pottery research brings cooking into view. Accounts from 1941, 1947 and 1965 describe smaller cooking vessels used for children’s porridge and larger pots for meat or vegetable relish. These are later observations from eastern Zimbabwe, not a claim that every family in the nineteenth century owned an identical kitchen set.

The same study describes potters, mainly women, carefully selecting clay from streams and riverbanks. Researchers combined archives with knowledge shared by Manyika elders and potters. That lets a broken vessel tell a richer story than its shape alone: someone had to recognize suitable clay, prepare it and turn it into a useful container.

At Chief Mugabe’s homestead near Great Zimbabwe in the late nineteenth century, travelers Theodore and Mabel Bent were given a kitchen rondavel for the night. It also contained a chicken enclosure. Their account gives one unusually specific glimpse of a room serving several purposes, with feathered fellow lodgers included.

A much later study, published in 1981, describes sun drying as an important way rural Shona households preserved food across the year. Its author also noted seasonal shortages of fresh produce. Food history therefore includes the work between harvest and dinner: drying and storing supplies mattered alongside growing them.

Written language sample: “nhanga” means “pumpkin.” George Fortune’s 1979 study reproduces this entry from the 1974 Standard Shona Dictionary. The same written form also names a house for unmarried girls in Zezuru usage. Context matters: a dictionary can keep you from mistaking a bedroom for a vegetable.

Printed dictionaries appeared during the colonial period: Hartmann’s English-Mashona Dictionary in 1894 and Elliot’s dictionary in 1897 used different selections and spellings. Fortune’s later review shows why these books must be read critically. Recording a language on paper did not mean its local varieties suddenly became identical.

British South Africa Company settlers entered Mashonaland in 1890. Colonial demands for labor and taxes, together with seizures of livestock and land, disrupted existing authority and livelihoods. This was a political takeover affecting distinct communities, not the peaceful beginning of society in a previously empty place.

Shona communities resisted Company rule during the wars of 1896 to 1897. Colonial forces destroyed crops and grain stores as part of their campaign. Those attacks show why the history of a war is also a history of family food supplies: losing a field could matter long after soldiers had moved away.

ending.text: Colonial conquest reduced the independence of Shona communities during the 1890s; 1914 is only this map record’s endpoint. Their languages, households and traditions continued and changed.
